paper.title: Epigenetically driven GAS2L3 enforces non-canonical cell cycle progression to promote osimertinib resistance in lung adenocarcinoma.
paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) have markedly improved outcomes in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), yet acquired resistance to the third-generation inhibitor osimertinib remains inevitable. Although metabolic reprogramming is increasingly recognized as a driver of therapeutic resistance, the epigenetic consequences of lactate accumulation and their functional relevance in osimertinib resistance are poorly understood. Here we report that osimertinib-resistant LUAD cells exhibit enhanced glycolytic flux, increased intracellular lactate levels, and elevated histone H4 lysine 8 lactylation (H4K8la). Integrative transcriptomic analysis revealed significant enrichment of cell-cycle-associated pathways in resistant tumors, despite downregulation of canonical Cyclin B1 and Cyclin D1. Among the upregulated genes, GAS2L3 emerged as a prominent candidate. Genome-wide CUT&Tag profiling demonstrated enrichment of H4K8la at the GAS2L3 promoter, which was confirmed by ChIP-qPCR. Functionally, GAS2L3 overexpression accelerated S/G2-M progression and promoted proliferation under drug pressure, whereas its silencing induced cell-cycle arrest and restored osimertinib sensitivity both in vitro and in xenograft models. Notably, resistant cells displayed elevated P53 expression without induction of its canonical effector P21, indicating checkpoint uncoupling and a noncanonical mode of cell-cycle regulation. Mechanistically, glycolysis inhibition reduced H4K8la and GAS2L3 expression and partially re-sensitized resistant cells, while exogenous lactate restored H4K8la levels and resistance phenotypes, establishing a metabolically driven epigenetic circuit. Clinically, high GAS2L3 expression was associated with shorter progression-free survival in osimertinib-treated patients. Collectively, our findings identify a glycolysis-H4K8la-GAS2L3 axis that drives noncanonical cell-cycle reprogramming independently of classical Cyclin-CDK activation, thereby promoting acquired osimertinib resistance. These results uncover a metabolism-epigenetics-cell cycle interface that may represent a therapeutic vulnerability in EGFR-mutant LUAD.

paper.title: Case Report: Longitudinal clonal evolution in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with coexisting MET exon 14 skipping and EML4-ALK fusion and subsequent KRAS/BRAF bypass mutations.
paper.abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer occurs through on-target mutations or bypass activation of alternative pathways. The longitudinal molecular evolution of a tumor across successive lines of therapy is rarely captured by repeat biopsy. We report a 68-year-old never-smoking woman with EGFR exon 19 deletion lung adenocarcinoma. First-line therapy achieved a partial response, with progression after 10.7 months; after 61 months of osimertinib, re-biopsy revealed concurrent EGFR T790M (9.3%), EML4-ALK fusion (E6:A20; 6.0%), and MET exon 14 skipping (c.3028G>T; 4.0%); aumolertinib plus ensartinib achieved stable disease for approximately 13 months. On further progression, a third biopsy showed molecular changes consistent with clonal evolution: the EML4-ALK fusion, MET exon 14 alteration, and EGFR T790M were no longer detected; the EGFR exon 19 deletion expanded to 47.71%; and KRAS G12R (10.17%), KRAS L19F (7.85%), BRAF D594N (8.13%), and BRAF E501K (6.38%) had emerged. Treatment with ivonescimab, a programmed cell death protein 1 and vascular endothelial growth factor bispecific antibody, plus pemetrexed and carboplatin, followed by pemetrexed plus ivonescimab, achieved stable disease; because chemotherapy was given concurrently, the contribution of ivonescimab cannot be isolated. PD-L1 (tumor proportion score <1%) was assessed on an earlier biopsy and blood tumor mutational burden was measured in 2019. This case is consistent with longitudinal clonal dynamics under sequential targeted therapy, namely regression of drug-sensitive clones and emergence of mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway bypass alterations, and the feasibility of an immunotherapy-containing regimen in a multi-driver tumor with unfavorable immune biomarkers.

paper.title: Case Report: Long-term survival of a patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring EGFR 19del/T790M/C797S and KIF26B-NTRK1 rearrangement.
paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene mutation stands as one of the most prevalent driver genetic alterations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). While targeted therapies against EGFR have substantially enhanced patient prognosis, acquired resistance remains a core challenge that limits therapeutic efficacy. Patients with stage IV NSCLC generally exhibit a dismal prognosis, with only about 7% of those with stage IVB disease surviving beyond five years. Herein, we report a case of a 47-year-old female patient diagnosed with advanced lung adenocarcinoma, whose clinical course has persisted for nearly a decade. Initial genetic testing identified an EGFR exon 19 deletion (19del). Following treatment with osimertinib, the patient developed concurrent cis-arranged EGFR T790M/C797S double mutations and a neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 1 (NTRK1) gene rearrangement. Subsequently, through a multimodal therapeutic strategy integrating local intervention, radiation therapy, and targeted therapy, the patient's disease has been sustainably controlled for several years, and she remains alive with stable clinical status to date. NTRK1 fusions are a well-defined mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR-TKIs, but they are uncommon. This case reports a KIF26B-NTRK1 rearrangement not previously described in lung cancer; however, its functional significance remains to be confirmed. The principal value of this report lies in the completeness of the longitudinal molecular and clinical record, which documents how an on-target mutation and a bypass rearrangement can coexist and persist.

paper.title: EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with leptomeningeal metastasis after osimertinib treatment: intrathecal chemotherapy combined with targeted therapy supported by cerebrospinal fluid next generation sequencing - a case report.
paper.abstract: Background: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a severe complication of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Conventional cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology has limited sensitivity and often delays diagnosis. We report a case of LM molecularly supported by CSF next-generation sequencing (NGS) after three negative cytological examinations. NGS also revealed a potential bypass resistance alteration that informed subsequent treatment considerations. Case: A 57-year-old female never-smoker had EGFR exon 21 p.L858R-mutant lung adenocarcinoma. After 18 months of first-line osimertinib (80 mg once daily), she developed progressive nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Contrast-enhanced cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed linear leptomeningeal enhancement. Lumbar puncture showed markedly elevated intracranial pressure (>300 mmH2O) and increased CSF protein. However, three CSF cytological examinations (including cell block sections) found no malignant cells. CSF NGS detected the EGFR p.L858R mutation identical to the primary tumor, together with CDK4 amplification. Integrated with the clinical and MRI presentation, these findings supported a diagnosis of probable LM and suggested cell-cycle bypass activation as a potential mechanism associated with osimertinib resistance. After intrathecal methotrexate plus continued oral osimertinib, her neurological symptoms improved markedly, and intracranial pressure returned to normal. The first seizure occurred on March 19, 2026, and MRI on April 8, 2026 confirmed new brain parenchymal metastases. Whole-brain radiotherapy with a local boost to the metastases, antiepileptic treatment, and continued osimertinib led to obvious shrinkage of the intracranial lesions. Grade 3 thrombocytopenia and severe malnutrition occurred during multimodal therapy and improved with supportive care. At the last follow-up, the patient was clinically stable with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of 1. Conclusions: CSF NGS can overcome the diagnostic bottleneck of cytology-negative LM. It can also identify potential resistance alterations and actionable targets (such as CDK4/6 inhibitors) at the same time, providing direction for subsequent targeted strategies. Conventional cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology has limited sensitivity and often delays diagnosis.
We report a case of LM molecularly supported by CSF next-generation sequencing (NGS) after three negative cytological examinations.
NGS also revealed a potential bypass resistance alteration that informed subsequent treatment considerations.
Case: A 57-year-old female never-smoker had EGFR exon 21 p.L858R-mutant lung adenocarcinoma.
After 18 months of first-line osimertinib (80 mg once daily), she developed progressive nausea, vomiting, and dizziness.
Contrast-enhanced cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed linear leptomeningeal enhancement.

paper.title: [Resistance Mechanisms and Recent Advances in the Third-generation EGFR-TKI Osimertinib for Non-small Cell Lung Cancer].
paper.abstract: Lung cancer is one of the malignant tumors with the highest morbidity and mortality worldwide, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of all lung cancer cases, with lung adenocarcinoma being the predominant histological subtype. Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) sensitizing mutations are among the most common and important actionable driver alterations in Chinese patients with lung adenocarcinoma, and the advent of EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) has inaugurated a new era of precision targeted therapy for lung adenocarcinoma. Osimertinib, a third-generation EGFR-TKI, has become the standard first-line treatment for advanced EGFR-mutated NSCLC and substantially improves survival; however, acquired resistance remains the central limitation to long-term benefit. This review first delineates the distinction between primary and acquired resistance, then summarizes the principal mechanisms underlying acquired resistance to Osimertinib, including EGFR-dependent alterations, bypass pathway activation, histological transformation and cellular plasticity, tumour microenvironment remodelling and metabolic reprogramming, as well as recently identified mechanisms such as SWI/SNF-related, matrix-associated, actin-dependent regulator of chromatin, subfamily A, member 4 (SMARCA4) loss, the YAP1/AXL axis and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) epigenetic adaptation. Based on the frequent co-occurrence of multiple resistance mechanisms, we further summarize clinical-scenario-based therapeutic strategies and representative domestic and international studies after resistance to third-generation EGFR-TKIs, so as to provide theoretical references for overcoming Osimertinib resistance. Overall, precise resistance profiling via rebiopsy and liquid biopsy, rational pathway-directed combination therapy, and the integration of next-generation EGFR inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates and patient-derived organoid drug sensitivity testing are expected to transform EGFR-mutated NSCLC from inevitable resistance into a manageable chronic disease. .

paper.title: [Retrospective Analysis of the Efficacy and Safety of Amivantamab-containing Regimens in Patients with EGFR-mutant Lung Cancer and Leptomeningeal Metastases].
paper.abstract: Background: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a devastating complication of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), occurring most frequently in patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant NSCLC. However, treatment options remain limited for patients who develop LM after treatment with the third-generation EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of Amivantamab-containing regimens in this patient population. Methods: A total of 11 patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC and LM who received Amivantamab-containing regimens at Peking Union Medical College Hospital between February 2025 and July 2026 were retrospectively included. Neurological symptoms, findings on contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology, LM-progression-free survival (PFS), and adverse events were evaluated. Follow-up for all patients was censored on July 31, 2026, with a median follow-up duration of 3.7 months (IQR: 2.1-7.0). Three patients had not yet reached the prespecified time point for their first standardized radiographic assessment by the data cutoff and were therefore censored in the follow-up analysis. Results: Among the 11 patients, 8 (72.7%) received Amivantamab in combination with a third-generation EGFR-TKI, whereas the remaining 3 patients received Amivantamab plus Pemetrexed, Amivantamab plus Zipalertinib, and Amivantamab monotherapy, respectively. Following treatment initiation, LM-related neurological symptoms improved in 8 patients (72.7%), with a time to symptom relief ranging from 1 to 7 days (median, 2.5 days). Among the 8 patients with evaluable post-baseline MRI, the best overall responses were complete response in 1 patient, partial response in 5 patients, and stable disease in 2 patients. Only three patients underwent post-treatment CSF cytologic reassessment; cytology clearance occurred in 2 patients and remained positive in 1 patient. During follow-up, 3 patients experienced disease progression, and 1 patient died before the first scheduled radiographic assessment. LM-PFS among the aforementioned 4 patients ranged from 1.7 to 9.7 months. Treatment-related adverse events were predominantly dermatologic/mucosal toxicities and infusion-related reactions. Two patients discontinued Amivantamab because of persistent dermatologic/mucosal toxicities and personal preference; one of these patients was rechallenged with Amivantamab after disease recurrence. No treatment-related deaths occurred. Conclusions: Amivantamab-containing multimodal treatment regimens were associated with symptom improvement and preliminary radiographic disease-control signals. However, because concomitant systemic therapies, intrathecal treatment, and CSF diversion procedures were present, the observed changes cannot be disentangled from or fully attributed to the independent effect of Amivantamab. The clinical benefit of Amivantamab in LM requires further validation in prospective studies.

paper.title: Structural Optimization of Pyrimidine-Based EGFR Inhibitors Against Resistance Mutations in NSCLC.
paper.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a major global health burden, particularly among non-smoking Asian populations, in whom activating EGFR mutations are the predominant oncogenic drivers. The emergence of multiple resistance mutations like the T790M, C797S, and especially the clinically intractable L858R/T790M/C797S triple mutant, has rendered all existing tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) ineffective. Despite substantial advances across three generations of EGFR-TKIs, the therapeutic options available for resistant mutations remain limited. Currently no approved agent is capable of selectively and effectively targeting the triple mutant EGFR. This unmet clinical need highlights the urgency for continued drug discovery efforts aimed at overcoming resistance mediated by the C797S mutation. This need has driven intensive efforts toward developing inhibitors capable of overcoming C797S-mediated resistance. Among the scaffolds explored, pyrimidine has emerged as particularly tractable, offering favorable ligand efficiency, synthetic accessibility and multiple substitution vectors that project into the T790M-remodeled hydrophobic pocket and the region vacated by Cys797, while engaging the conserved Met793 of the hinge region. This review presents, an overview of the key structural features of the EGFR's ATP-binding site is provided to facilitate a deeper understanding of the rational design of future EGFR inhibitors.

paper.title: Osimertinib resistance in non-small cell lung cancer is mediated by sustained AKT activation through lipid raft-dependent insulin signaling.
paper.abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a major challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Using an osimertinib-resistant (AR) cell model lacking the on-target EGFR C797S mutation, we uncover sustained AKT phosphorylation under osimertinib treatment driven by insulin receptor (INSR) signaling. Notably, INSR-AKT activation is observed exclusively in AR cells, whereas parental H1975 cells fail to activate AKT even following INSR overexpression or exogenous insulin stimulation. Cholesterol depletion abolishes the INSR-AKT response in AR cells, indicating a lipid raft-dependent mechanism. Consistently, INSR localizes within lipid rafts in AR but not in parental H1975 cells. Proteomic profiling reveals the enrichment of lipid raft-associated proteins in AR cells. Among them, flotillin-1 (FLOT1) is identified as a key raft scaffold mediating INSR-AKT signaling and osimertinib resistance through functional shRNA screening. Co-immunoprecipitation and proximity ligation assay confirm a cholesterol-dependent interaction between FLOT1 and INSR. paper.title: Management of Advanced EGFR-Mutant Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer Across the Disease Course.
paper.abstract: Advances in targeted therapy have improved outcomes for patients with advanced epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors and first-line combination regimens have expanded treatment options, making the balance between survival benefit, toxicity, treatment burden, and individual patient fitness increasingly important in initial treatment selection. As acquired resistance continues to limit the duration of benefit, this decision must also be considered in the context of subsequent care. At progression, tissue and plasma profiling provide complementary information that can help characterize the diverse mechanisms of resistance and guide further treatment. As resistance-directed therapies and antibody-drug conjugates expand the available treatment options, their selection requires consideration of prior therapy and the pattern of progression, together with molecular findings where relevant. This review examines these interconnected decisions across the course of advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC, from first-line treatment selection to the assessment and management of acquired resistance. We also address central nervous system involvement, uncommon EGFR mutations, and exon 20 insertions as distinct clinical settings in which disease distribution and the underlying molecular alteration shape treatment choices. By integrating clinical and translational evidence, we discuss how these factors may inform treatment sequencing and individualized care, with attention to survival, quality of life, and the cumulative burden of therapy across the disease course.
